## How to read this

Every slide says which of three things it is talking about, because they are easy to blur:

| Mark | Means |
|---|---|
| **In the player** | Code under `sieve_player/` or `tests/` that runs when you use SIEVE |
| **In the simulation** | `docs/playground/sim/`: the real store code run against a simulated clock, disk and memory |
| **On paper** | `docs/playground/contract.md` or the journal: a decision nothing runs yet |

The simulation's desktop figures are measured on this machine. Its laptop, HPC and disk-rate
figures are guesses and are labelled so where they appear.

Sources: `docs/playground/JOURNAL.md`, `contract.md`, `figures.md`, `adversary.md`,
`adversary-2.md`, `docs/findings/window-against-full.md`, and `git log v5..HEAD`.

## What you asked for

To stop thinking about the back end. Today a new tool means touching several holders to be sure
nothing broke. Four goals, in your words:

1. Windows are reliable and fast.
2. A saved file opens where the user left off.
3. Walk bare and walk clip keep working as tools are added.
4. What is likely to be revisited does not cost the user much.

Both ends of hardware are real: a collaborator's weak machine, where a big enough pipeline must
be slow and never fail, and an HPC node, which SIEVE should fill.

# Where the tree stood

## Before: many holders, each with its own rules {.smaller}

*In the player, at `v5` (`b23ff2c4`), from the stage 1 inventory.*

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart LR
  T[A tool's result] --> M[memo<br/>4 GB constant]
  T --> D[decoder cache<br/>4 GB constant]
  T --> S[four walk stacks<br/>512 MB each]
  T --> H[held runs + pickle file<br/>512 MB]
  T --> W[window.py<br/>four result dicts]
  T --> B[bare temp folder<br/>never removed]
  T --> C[cut clips, csv,<br/>periods JSON, frame-times]
```

Each has its own use of the key, its own bound, its own staleness rule and its own writer.
Seven constants bound them, none read off the machine, about 10.5 GB by default.

The cost of that showed in one number: the period tool (PR #33, 81 commits) touched `window` 26
times, `walk` 14, `worker` 12, `held` 12, `graph` 12, `plan` 11, `heldwalks` 11. Two plain frame
tools (PRs #26, #27) touched nothing outside `tools/` and `tests/`.

## The six oracles, and how `v5` did against them {.smaller}

These are the invariants the whole effort is held to.

| | Oracle | At `v5` |
|---|---|---|
| O1 | What is served for an address equals a cold recompute of it | **Fails twice**: tool code is in no key; the footage print was size plus the first and last MB |
| O2 | Dropping any entry that is not a checkpoint changes speed and nothing else | **Fails** for a gate-fed period and a region's served clip: they are sources, and nothing remakes them |
| O3 | A checkpoint is served after reopen, or said to be gone; never a wrong one | No referent; the held file's loss is silent |
| O4 | Adding a tool changes no file of the store, the walk or the monitor | Holds only for a frame tool of existing types |
| O5 | Memory stays under the budget; too small a budget is said, not crashed on | **Fails**: seven constants, library threads uncapped |
| O6 | Two processes writing one address leave one whole entry | Holds for frame-times and clips, not the held file |

# The idea

## The hypothesis: one address, one store, one ask

*On paper (`contract.md`), then in the simulation.*

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart LR
  subgraph Callers
    A1[window]
    A2[clip walk]
    A3[bare walk]
    A4[cluster job]
    A5[csv write]
    A6[a gate]
  end
  Callers -->|ask: key + row| ASK{{the ask}}
  ASK -->|hit| ST[(one store)]
  ASK -->|miss: compute, then put| ST
  ST --- MEM[memory tier]
  ST --- DSK[disk tier<br/>chunks of rows, a file each]
  CP[checkpoint<br/>manifest of addresses<br/>+ document snapshot] -.never let go.-> DSK
```

The keys were already right and already one (`plan.py`). What was missing: one place results
live, under one budget, and one way to ask for a result without knowing whether it is held or
must be made. A tool does nothing about any of it.

## Decisions made at the start {.smaller}

| | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | A checkpoint is bound to its key and carries a snapshot of the document | A frozen result served under changed settings breaks O1 |
| D2 | Saving promises checkpointed results only; everything else is a cache | The tree had nothing called a pinned result; the checkpoint is coined |
| D5 | One budget of memory, cores and disk, read off the machine, overridable | Small is the weak laptop, large is the HPC node |
| D6 | Safe under many writers: a uniquely named temporary, then one atomic rename | Processes and cluster nodes on one filesystem |
| D7 | Stage 3 is a deterministic simulation, not a model | The code that passes is the code that ships; a failure replays from its seed |

# The simulation

## How the simulation works

*In the simulation (`sim/sim.py`, `sim/store.py`, now `sieve_player/result_store.py`).*

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart TB
  SEED[a seed] --> RUN[60 doings of a user:<br/>scrub, walk, edit, edit code,<br/>change footage, evict, delete files,<br/>reopen, crash mid-walk,<br/>a second process, checkpoint, restore]
  RUN --> STORE[the real store code]
  STORE --> DISK[simulated disk + clock<br/>crash between the two steps of a write]
  RUN --> CHECK{after every doing}
  WORLD[World.truth:<br/>digest of everything a value<br/>really depends on] --> CHECK
  SCHEME[Scheme.key:<br/>what this design puts in a key] --> STORE
  CHECK --> O[O1, O3, O5, O6]
  CHECK -->|a break| SHRINK[shrunk to the<br/>shortest failing sequence]
```

A design is a *scheme*: what it puts in the key and how it writes. The same seeds are played
against each scheme, so designs are compared on identical histories.

## Result: the oracles have teeth

*In the simulation. 150 seeds of 60 doings each.*

| Scheme | Outcome |
|---|---|
| The contract's | No oracle broken |
| Tool code left out of the key, as `v5` | O1 broken by: scrub, edit code, a second process walks |
| Footage print of size and ends, as `v5` | O1 broken by: scrub, footage changes in its middle, walk |
| Entries written in place | O1 broken by a crash mid-walk, twice |

The first run also broke O5 in my own store: memory let go before inputs were read was filled
again by reading them. The fix is a **reservation**: work under way takes its output and its
live inputs out of the one budget. `graph.py`'s `Ref` and the "pinned" memo entries are that
same double count, unsolved in `v5`.

## Measured figures that changed the design {.smaller}

*Measured on this desktop (i9-14900KF, 64 GB, NVMe), gathered from `docs/findings/` by run 2.*

| What | Figure | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| A seek | 80 to 140 ms at 1080p, 490 ms at 5.3K | One seek is fifty to a hundred rows read in order (1.1 to 2.8 ms each). Scrub latency is seeks, not tools |
| Cores inside one clip | 7.03 ms a row at one worker, 2.05 at four and at eight, worse at sixteen | Work flattens near four. An HPC node is filled across pieces that share nothing, a process each |
| A bigger memo | 515 rows/s under 64 MB, 151 to 316 under 4 GB | Holding more made a walk slower. "Fill the RAM" is wrong for planes passing through |
| A plane | about 2 ms and 2 MB a row at 1080p | Cheap to make, dear to keep: writing it to a 100 MB/s disk costs ten times recomputing it |
| A table or signal | a track step is 0.6 to 0.9 ms for 1.2 KB; a signal is 4 B | The reverse: always worth keeping |

## The policy that came out of it

*In the simulation; it is the contract's.*

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart LR
  V[a value, with the seconds<br/>it took to make,<br/>inputs included] --> Q{cost against<br/>its own write}
  Q -->|many times its write:<br/>tables, signals, whole results| DISK[(disk, at once)]
  Q -->|at least its write:<br/>a slow plane| SECOND[disk, the second time<br/>it is made, into free room only]
  Q -->|less: an ordinary plane| MEMONLY[memory only,<br/>into free memory,<br/>pushes nothing out]
```

Memory lets go of what saves the fewest seconds a byte (GreedyDual-Size, Cao and Irani 1997).
Disk lets go of what was touched longest ago. Neither lets go of what a checkpoint names.

The second adversary's analysis: once admission is the same, GreedyDual-Size against plain
recency changes little on disk. **Admission is the policy.**

## Result: what the policy buys {.smaller}

*In the simulation. An hour of 1080p, an ants-like pipeline. Desktop measured; laptop a guess.*

"lru" is the naive reading of the hypothesis: one budgeted store that holds by recency and
writes everything.

| | Policy | lru |
|---|---|---|
| First walk, desktop | **392 s** | 1049 s |
| First walk, laptop | **1031 s** | 11386 s |
| Same walk again, or a reopened file's walk | **under 20 s** everywhere | 1989 s on the laptop, and the checkpoint is refused |
| A detect nudge, three in a row, desktop | 106 s, then 59, then 51 | 52 each time |

<div style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.6em">
First walk, laptop:
<div style="background:#2a7; width:9%; color:#fff; padding:2px 6px; white-space:nowrap">policy 1031 s</div>
<div style="background:#c44; width:100%; color:#fff; padding:2px 6px">lru 11386 s</div>
</div>

The first nudge is slower under the policy: that is the price of not writing planes on a
guess. It is repaid by the second.

## Result: where each loses

*In the simulation.*

**Why lru loses.** Planes fill the disk and push the tables off it. At 5.3K the desktop's same
walk again costs 9711 s and the checkpoint is refused with 14296 of 21706 entries gone. One
store with one recency order is *worse than today's separate holders*. So the policy is the
design, not a tuning.

**Where the policy still loses.** The laptop at 5.3K: 21476 s for every nudge, since 40 GB of
disk holds almost none of the gray planes. Slow and never failing, which is what you asked of
small machines. A region or a scale on the pipeline is the user's lever there, not the store's.

**What the store cannot help.** A scrub while building is one seek and one row: 103 ms on the
desktop, 526 ms at 5.3K. A decoder reading ahead can lower that; the store cannot.

# Trying to break it

## Two adversaries

*Runs 5 and 6: an Opus session told to prove each break with a script, not to argue it.*

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart LR
  A1[Adversary 1<br/>against the contract<br/>and the simulated store] -->|8 proved breaks,<br/>4 of them holes in<br/>my own oracles| F1[mended in<br/>store.py and sim.py]
  A2[Adversary 2<br/>against the store on real files:<br/>real processes, kills, a held lock] -->|12 items,<br/>11 proved| F2[mended in<br/>folder.py]
  F1 --> R[its scripts run again<br/>after the mending]
  F2 --> R
```

The most useful finding of the first: the torture never filled the disk. `_make_room` ran zero
times in 150 seeds, and mutants that ignored the budget passed. The torture's disks are now 1
to 40 GB with an oracle on the disk's use.

## What the adversaries changed {.smaller}

| Found | Now |
|---|---|
| A checkpoint looked for its entries, then named them; one went in between | The manifest lands as **pending** first, then the look, then it is finished |
| A checkpoint too big was refused only after three rounds of filling | Sizes are summed and refused **before any work**, with the figures |
| A demand kept every value alive outside the budget: 10.4 GB under a 3 GB budget | A value is alive under a reservation or in the store, nowhere else |
| The chunk grid was not in the key | The grid is the node's own and part of the entry's name |
| Parts torn by a crash counted as used for good | A part older than a grace is let go |
| Windows will not rename over a file another process has open | Passed over, not an error |
| A lock judged stale by comparing two machines' clocks | Stale by this process's own monotonic clock |
| A put was 6 ms whatever its size (the flush) | Only what a checkpoint names is flushed; a torn entry is caught by length and checksum |

Of the second adversary's twelve: nine no longer reproduce, one raced case is 0 of 300, and one
was not seen to finish.

# What you corrected

## Windows are best effort

*Your words, 2026-11-21. I had assumed a window shows exactly what a key names. That was false.*

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart LR
  subgraph clip[the whole clip]
    direction LR
    L[rows before] --- E1[edge:<br/>within reach] --- IN[inner rows of the window:<br/>EXACT, the full walk's to reuse] --- E2[edge:<br/>within reach] --- R[rows after]
  end
  E1 -.window's own value.-> WM[memory only,<br/>addressed with its range,<br/>never answers a full walk]
  E2 -.window's own value.-> WM
  IN -.exact value.-> ST[(the store)]
```

The rule runs one way. A window's value never answers an exact ask (a full walk, a checkpoint,
a bare walk). An exact value may answer a window.

No new declaration was needed: every tool already says how far it reads (`reach_in_rows`).

## Result: the rule tried on every tool

*In the player. Run 7 as a one-off (`docs/findings/window-against-full.md`), run 9 as a test.*

- Of 39 registered tools, **38 hold**; `file` is skipped.
- `smooth` differs from the full walk at **exactly** the rows its reach of (2, 2) puts outside
  the window, and matches where the window touches the clip's start.
- Run 9 made it a test over the registry: `tests/test_window_against_full.py`, 40 cases. A tool
  with a wrong or missing reach fails by name. Five tools that declared no reach got one.

What it does not show, in the run's own words: a tool with an unbounded side allows every row,
so `track`, `kinematics`, `tracks_filter` and `resolve` are not tested by it.

This is the slice nearest your goal: a tool added next month is in the test without anyone
remembering.

## A loop: planes against proxies {.smaller}

*Measured on the crossings clip (`sim/proxyrate.py`), priced in the simulation (`sim/loop.py`).*

In `v5` a looped row the memo let go was made again by the worker on every pass, so a loop that
did not fit the memo recomputed for ever.

| | Planes | Proxies (1280x720 jpeg) |
|---|---|---|
| One 1080p frame | 6.2 MB | 70 KB, 2.2 ms to make, 2.0 ms to show |
| One 5.3K frame | 47.6 MB | 70 KB, 4.7 ms to make |
| A ten second loop, 1080p | 1.8 GB | 0.02 GB |
| A ten second loop, 5.3K | 13.8 GB | 0.02 GB |
| Laptop, 5.3K, one view, a pass | 24 s | 1.5 s |
| Laptop, 5.3K, two views, a pass | 419 s | 3.0 s |

Decided: planes when the loop's rows fit free memory, proxies when they do not; never a plane
made again each pass. A proxy is never handed to a tool.

**In the player** since run 8 (`window.py`, 110 lines, two seam tests). You have not yet said
what you saw of it.

## The plan turned over

*On paper. The first framing, three holders as one problem, was wrong; your check-ins found it.*

I had planned to move the held file onto the store first. An Opus read of `held.py` said:

- It **already does** what the contract wrote as new: it reuses a row only when what its reach
  read of the walk's and the cut's edges is the same. It is the range-aware holder, working.
- Its file sits beside the document and goes where the document goes. That is what makes a
  saved file open where you left off. A store under `%LOCALAPPDATA%` does not.
- It is small (5 to 9 bytes a row a node) and about twenty call sites lean on it.

So moving it first would spend the most seams on the smallest bytes. `held.py` and your ticked
decision on held results stay untouched. The store went under the **bare walk** instead.

# What landed

## In the player: the bare walk keeps its rows

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart LR
  BW[bare walk<br/>bare.py] --> G[Graph._compute<br/>a frame node's row]
  G -->|memo miss: ask| K[Keeper<br/>result_keeper.py]
  G -->|row made: tell| K
  K -->|a chunk of 256 rows| S[Store<br/>result_store.py]
  S --> F[Folder<br/>result_folder.py<br/>length + crc32, flush, rename]
  F --> D[(app folder/results<br/>20 GiB, SIEVE_RESULTS)]
  ADDR[address = raw key + cut + reach<br/>+ code of the tool and all upstream<br/>+ sieve_player, numpy, cv2<br/>+ digest of the whole footage file] -.-> K
```

Only a bare walk has a keeper; the window's Graph has none, so nothing a window shows changed.
Only small rows of frame nodes are kept (tables, scalars), never planes.

**Result**, crossings clip, three bare walks as separate processes over one folder:
**2.5 s, then 0.9 s and 0.9 s**, all four result nodes equal field by field, 5.8 MB kept.
Ten seconds of clip is too short to price; a long walk has not been timed.

# Where it stands

## Against your four goals

| Goal | In the player | Not yet |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Windows reliable and fast | Budgets off the machine; loop proxies; window checked against full walk for every tool | The store is not under the window. Speed is not shown: the simulation cannot see the GUI thread or the GIL |
| 2. A saved file opens where left off | Nothing new. `held.py` does this today, untouched | The checkpoint exists in the contract and the simulation only |
| 3. Bare and clip walks keep working as tools are added | The registry-wide test: a wrong reach fails by name | Cold-twice and cold-against-warm are not registry-wide |
| 4. Revisiting costs little | A bare walk keeps frame rows: 2.5 s to 0.9 s | Series and stepped nodes, `track` above all; a bare walk never walks cuts in time |

The store is sound and has one caller. The published path was already safe by brute force: a
bare walk in `v5` reuses nothing.

## What I now think is wrong {.smaller}

Found today by putting your three hypotheticals (period algebra, a few thousand periods, a
Morlet tool) against the contract.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart LR
  subgraph tree[The tree's memo, since before this branch]
    T1[address = key, row,<br/>what the value READ of its cut's edges]
    T1 --> T2[row 5000 of a row-by-row tool<br/>has one address in period P,<br/>in P and Q's overlap, or in no period]
  end
  subgraph mine[The contract and the keeper]
    C1[address holds<br/>THE CUT it was made inside]
    C1 --> C2[the overlap shares nothing with P;<br/>thousands of periods are<br/>thousands of tiny files]
  end
```

- **The contract's line on the cut is coarser than the tree.** Not incorrect, only wasteful: it
  errs toward recomputing, never toward a wrong answer. One line to change, and the keeper's
  address to follow `cut.read` as the memo's does.
- **The keeper decides "image, never keep" by array shape.** A scalogram is two-dimensional,
  costly and small. The contract's own rule, seconds saved per byte, gets it right.
- **Stepped state is not saved at chunk edges**, though the contract says a walk resumes from
  the last chunk held. A tracker restarts from its cut's first row.
- **Unchecked:** whether the registry's types can carry a period set as a value, a two-input
  gate, or a time-by-scale matrix.

## Robust against wrong, not against slow

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart TB
  A[An address can miss two ways] --> FINE[holds LESS than the value depends on]
  A --> COARSE[holds MORE than the value depends on]
  FINE --> WRONG[a stale answer is served:<br/>silent, never seen by eye]
  COARSE --> SLOW[something is made again:<br/>seen as slowness]
  style WRONG fill:#f6d5d5
  style SLOW fill:#fdf3c7
```

Every rule in the contract leans to the right-hand side on purpose. If "dropping any entry
changes time and nothing else" holds, the store can make a future tool slow but cannot make it
wrong. That is a design claim: proven in the simulation, exercised by one caller in the player.

It says nothing about a tracker that does not exist yet, and building toward a guess at its
storage would be the runtime shaping the model.

## How you tell, without reading the back end

Three checks that need to know nothing about the tool:

| Check | A failure means | Exists today |
|---|---|---|
| Walk it cold twice; compare | The tool is not a function of what it declared | A one-off on one real document (`bare_walk_thrice.py`) |
| Walk it cold, then warm; compare | The store served something it should not have | A test for one chain (gray, threshold, detect, count) |
| A window against the full walk | The declared reach is wrong | **Every registered tool** |

And one count per node, rows made against rows read back. After an edit at node X, everything
downstream of X is made and everything else is read back.

- Made where it should be read back: the address is too coarse. Slow.
- Read back where it should be made: a stale answer. The dangerous one.

That count exists only inside a test. A bare walk does not print it. What none of this catches:
a tool that reads an undeclared file passes all three until the file moves.

## Open, and yours to decide

None of these blocks the work.

- **Code beside the key, not in it.** An address would be a key, a code and a row; an entry of
  other code is served marked stale, which is your `!`; an exact walk asks for this code only.
  Proposed, not built: it meets your ticked decision that held results outlive a tool edit.
- **Where bare-walk results live**, and the 20 GiB figure.
- **A csv written from a window's card** is the window's, not exact. Whether the card says so.
- **The encoder's version is not in a cut file's key.** Two bakes gave the same bytes on this
  machine and this ffmpeg; across versions it is not shown.
- **`tests/test_graph.py`**: one test failed once in run 8 and passed after; the run says it
  asserts wall time and is not marked `simulation`.
- **`window.py:81`** may unpack four fields of a six-field run; unrun.

## What I would do next

1. Correct the contract's line on the cut to "what it read of its cut", and the keeper's
   address with it.
2. Make cold-twice and cold-against-warm run over the registry, as the window check does, and
   have a bare walk print rows made against rows read back.
3. Then the queued slice: series and stepped nodes under the keeper, `track` above all.

The first two turn "is it handled" from my account into something you run.

## One caveat on the machine

A bare walk of the whole camera file died of access violations at rows that moved, on `v5` as
on this branch, and so did loops of plain Python. The same evening Windows stopped with a
bugcheck. The evidence is in
`docs/findings/2026-11-21-bare-walk-crashes-on-the-full-file.md`.

That the processor is the cause is a hypothesis, not a finding: no core was isolated and no
memory test was run. It is the reason no long walk has been timed on this branch, and it is not
an explanation to reach for when a check fails.

## What it was, how it changed {.smaller}

*The player only. "Same" rows are as much the state of the branch as the changed ones.*

| | At `v5` | On this branch | |
|---|---|---|---|
| What bounds a holder | Seven constants, about 10.5 GB, none read off the machine | Each holder's limit shared out of half the machine's RAM, the constants as ceilings | Changed |
| Which footage a file is | Its size and its first and last MB | Those plus 32 slices through it; a bare walk's kept rows by a digest of every byte | Changed |
| A loop that outgrows the memo | Every row made again on every pass | Painted from display proxies, 70 KB a row | Changed |
| A window against the full walk | Nothing checked it; five tools declared no reach | A test over every registered tool, 40 cases; a wrong reach fails by name | Changed |
| A bare walk run a second time | Reuses nothing; full cost every time | Reads back a frame node's small rows: 2.5 s, then 0.9 s on the crossings clip | Changed |
| Tool code and library versions in an address | In no key | In the address of a bare walk's kept rows; still not in `plan.py`'s key, by your ticked decision | Partly |
| Results on disk under many writers | The held file, appended in place | A store with atomic, checksummed entries and a folder lock, called by the bare walk alone | Partly |
| A bare walk's series and stepped nodes, `track` above all | Made every walk | Made every walk | Same |
| A bare walk and cuts in time | Never walks them | Never walks them | Same |
